opus-5.5.text:
I think about it as a portfolio of my time, and honestly the weights have shifted a lot as the company has grown.

In the very early days, I was writing a lot of code myself. When you're a handful of people, the CEO is basically another engineer who also happens to do fundraising and talk to users. I think that's necessary. If you don't understand the product at the level of the actual implementation, you can't make good strategic calls, because you don't know what's cheap and what's expensive, what's a two-day hack and what's a six-month research problem.

As the team grew, I realized my leverage changed. One great hire can do far more than I could by writing a few more features. So recruiting became, I'd say, the single most important thing I do. If I had to put a number on it, at certain stages it was probably a third or more of my time: sourcing, having long conversations, convincing people who had very good offers elsewhere. The quality of the team sets the ceiling for everything else.

Strategy is interesting because it doesn't take that many hours, but it takes a lot of focus. Deciding what *not* to do is often the hardest part. In AI especially, the landscape changes every few months, so you have to keep re-evaluating where the real opportunity is. I try to protect some quiet time for that instead of letting meetings eat everything.

And I still stay hands-on, just in a different way. I'm not shipping production code every day anymore, but I use the product constantly, I look at what users generate, I read feedback, and I'll still dig into technical details with the team when something matters. I think founders who completely detach from the product lose their intuition pretty fast.

So my rough answer: recruiting is the multiplier, strategy is the direction, and hands-on involvement is what keeps both of them grounded in reality. You can't really drop any of the three. You just keep rebalancing as the company changes.

r001.rationale: The response says recruiting took “a third or more” of the CEO’s time at certain stages, but it does not specifically assign recruiting 40 percent of attention.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've gone back and forth on a lot, and honestly my answer has changed as the company has grown.

Early on, when we were just a handful of people, I was deep in the code. I'd written most of the original Taichi compiler myself, so being hands-on wasn't really a choice, it was just what the company was. And I think that was right for that stage. When you're trying to figure out whether something works at all, the fastest way to learn is to build it yourself.

But at some point I realized that the thing limiting the company wasn't how much I could personally do, it was how many great people we had. So recruiting moved up a lot in my priorities. I'd say for a technical founder it's probably the hardest transition, because writing code gives you immediate feedback and recruiting gives you very delayed feedback. You spend a month talking to someone, and you don't know if it worked out until a year later.

The way I think about it now is roughly in three layers. Strategy is deciding where we're going, and that's something I can't really delegate. Recruiting is making sure we have the people who can actually get us there, and I spend a surprising amount of time on it, probably more than most people would guess. And hands-on involvement is more selective now. I'll go deep on something when it's genuinely uncertain and the team needs a decision from someone who understands the details, or when I just need to stay close enough to the technology that I'm not making strategy decisions based on stale intuition.

That last part matters more than people think. If a CEO completely stops being hands-on, their judgment about what's possible starts to drift. So I try to keep one foot in, but I've accepted that my job is no longer to be the best engineer in the room. It's to make sure the best engineers want to be in the room.

r001.rationale: The response says recruiting takes a surprising amount of time but does not assign it 40 percent of the CEO’s attention.

astra-6.text:
I think recruiting is one of the highest-leverage things a CEO can do, but it’s hard to separate it from strategy. You need to know what you’re trying to achieve before you can decide who you need to hire. And you need enough hands-on involvement to understand where the real bottlenecks are.

The balance changes as the company grows. Early on, you have to do a lot yourself. Over time, your job becomes finding people who can take ownership and giving them the context to make good decisions. I’d stay close enough to the work to ask useful questions, while making sure I’m not becoming the bottleneck for the team.

r001.rationale: The response says recruiting is one of the CEO’s highest-leverage activities but does not assign it 40 percent of the CEO’s attention across the three areas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think recruiting is one of the highest-leverage things a CEO can do, but it’s closely connected to strategy and hands-on work. You need a clear strategy to know whom to hire, and you need enough involvement in the work to understand what capabilities the team is missing.

The balance changes as the company grows. Early on, you have to do a lot yourself. As you bring in strong people, your role shifts toward giving them context and ownership. I still think it’s useful to go deep on important problems, but the goal is to help the team make better decisions, rather than become the person every decision depends on.

r001.rationale: The response calls recruiting one of a CEO’s highest-leverage activities, but does not assign it 40 percent of the CEO’s attention.
